Such rhetoric coming from positions of influence institutionalizes exclusion and fosters xenophobia. Mr. President, this situation constitutes clear discrimination on the basis of religion. We urge this Council to take cognizance and reaffirm that freedom of religion and equality before the law are non-derogable rights. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you. My apologies, the last speaker was International Action for Peace and Sustainable Development by video. And that was the last speaker we could accommodate. With this last intervention, we have concluded the general debate under Item 9. Distinguished colleagues, I understand that a number of delegations have requested to exercise the right of reply on agenda Item 9. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Lithuania. You have three minutes.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. I am exercising this right of reply in response to the statement made by the delegation of Belarus during the item 9 general debate today. I would like to point out that Lithuania takes its international obligations very seriously. We are committed to the protection of refugees, especially those escaping conflict and persecution in their countries of origin. However, we do not and will not tolerate the instrumentalization of migrants for political purposes. There is a clear distinction between regular, irregular, and instrumentalized migration. Belarusian authorities are directly involved in organizing artificial flow of irregular migration with aim to exert political pressure on its neighbors. Belarus deliberately and inhumanly put the lives and well-being of migrants in danger, including women, children, and those persons with vulnerable situations. Lithuania has protested such actions and inactions as grave violations of the protocol against the smuggling of migrants by land, sea, and air, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, the protocol, which both Lithuania and Belarus are parties to. Moreover, Belarus has demonstrated a clear unwillingness to assist Lithuania and other European countries in combating migrant smuggling. Its border control agencies have repeatedly rejected Lithuania's requests for cooperation to suppress the smuggling of migrants. As a result, on 19 May 2025, Lithuania instituted proceedings against Belarus before the International Court of Justice. Lithuania contends that organized smuggling of migrants through Belarus to Lithuania is a transnational offense involving an organized criminal group, triggering the applicability of the protocol. Belarus' facilitation of mass illegal migration is a direct affront to principles of sovereign equality, territorial integrity, and non-intervention in the domestic affairs of other states. I thank you.
I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sudan. You have three minutes.

Thank you, Vice-President. We exercise the right of reply following unfounded erroneous information provided by the Center for Gender Justice and Women's Empowerment, Egypt Peace for Development and Human Rights, Japan Society for History Books, and other NGOs, which have used their presence here to launch propaganda campaigns against Sudan and undermine our policies. They are backed by militias which we are aware of, which hide behind Sudanese army factions. Sudan is committed to the Convention, and what we have heard is inaccurate. Sudan's army has its own system governing military operations. The army respects international human rights standards. The very structure of Sudan's army throughout represents the whole of Sudanese society and prohibits any ethnic or racial discrimination. What we have heard, therefore, runs counter to reality. These allegations were put forward by certain external parties. Sudan's army is committed to remedying the difficult situation in our country. We remind all NGOs that the militias that they seek to defend were the originators of massacres, including in Darfur. These NGOs must therefore stop spreading false information and document any violations committed in the north of Darfur and in the IDP camps by these militias. The camps are suffering violations because of the actions of rebel militias, despite our calls for peace. We have noted all of these horrors, and Sudan remains committed to promoting and protecting human rights and combating the rebel militias. We reserve the right to make criminal complaints against parties which use the Council.

This was the last speaker on my list. Is there any other delegation requesting to exercise the right of reply? I see none. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, with this last intervention, we have concluded the considerations of agenda item 9. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, I declare open item 10 of the agenda entitled Technical Assistance and Capacity Building. We will now hold the interactive dialogue on the High Commissioner's oral update with the participation of the independent human rights expert on the situation of human rights in Haiti. according to the Council Resolution 58/32. It is my honor to welcome Mr. Volker Turk, High Commissioner for Human Rights and the Independent Human Rights Expert on Haiti. Mr. William O'Neil, who is joining us by video and VTC. The list of speakers will close in 15 minutes. I now give the floor to the High Commissioner for Human Rights for his presentation.

Madam Vice-President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, The human rights situation in Haiti has reached a boiling point. Since my last update to this Council in March, violence and human rights violations and abuses have escalated and intensified. I welcome yesterday's decision of the UN Security Council to strengthen the Multinational Security Support Mission by transitioning it to the Gang Suppression Force for Haiti. This is a strong signal of support for the Haitian people. International commitment and backing for this are urgent. Without them, the worst may yet to come for Haiti and the broader region. More than 16,000 people have been killed and some 7,000 people injured in armed violence since the 1st of January 2022. And that's when we began our monitoring on gang-related violence. Today, gangs are spreading fear beyond the capital, Port-au-Prince, into nearby regions, including in the Lower Artibonite and in the Center Department. This violence is fertile ground for further cross-border arms, drugs, and human trafficking, which threaten to destabilize the wider subregion. An estimated 270,000 to 500,000 firearms are circulating illegally in Haiti, with most weapons in the hands of gangs. Gangs are killing and kidnapping people, extorting them at illegal checkpoints, hijacking trucks transporting food and other supplies, and burning and destroying homes, hospitals, schools, and public buildings. They are committing widespread sexual violence to assert dominance and territorial influence and displace people. The gangs kidnap women and girls and subject them to extreme brutality, including killing and sexual exploitation. My office is working with the authorities to step up investigations and prosecutions, including through specialized judicial units. I urge your strong support for programs to protect survivors of sexual violence. Madame la Vice-Présidente, le.

Madam Vice-President, the humanitarian toll is horrendous. Half of the population, 6 million souls, including 3.3 million children, need humanitarian aid. Around 1.3 million people, half of whom are children, once again, have fled their homes. Haiti is now among the five most worrying areas in the world. in terms of food insecurity. I am deeply concerned about the fate of children in Haiti. According to UNICEF, one child in seven does not go to school and that around another million children are at risk of dropping out of school. Furthermore, more and more children are victims of trafficking, victims of exploitation and forced recruitment, and this by gangs that sometimes use as They are used, in fact, as messengers, as people who are on the lookout, even people who bear weapons and have to fight against rival gangs, as well as against security forces and so-called self-defense units. We cannot imagine the long-term impact that all this is having on the children of Haiti and for Haitian society as a whole. In July, the authorities opened the first transit and guidance center in Port-au-Prince to provide temporary refuge and support for the reintegration of children who formerly belonged to armed gangs. We need more of these kinds of measures.

Distinguished participants, I am concerned that state law enforcement have used unnecessary and disproportionate lethal force in their operations against the gangs. For example, operations by law enforcement account for more than half of killings and injuries so far this year, a steep increase compared to 2024. Almost one third of people killed or injured were hit by stray bullets. Specialized police units have summarily executed 174 people this year for alleged affiliations with gangs. Since March, the government has stepped up its use of explosive drones in its anti-gang operations in Port-au-Prince. As of mid-September, drone strikes have killed at least 559 people, including 11 children. Most of these drone strikes are likely unlawful under international human rights law. The use of force by police and security personnel needs to respect the principles of legality, necessity, proportionality, non-discrimination, precaution, and accountability. I urge the authorities to investigate all allegations of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force and ensure perpetrators, regardless of affiliation, are brought to justice. It is deeply worrying that so-called self-defense groups and spontaneous crowds of people have killed more than 500 alleged gang members this year, with the alleged support of police officers. A spiral of violence between gang members, the population, and the security forces will only add to people's feelings of insecurity. Efforts to restore security need to be rooted in human rights and go hand in hand with rebuilding the rule of law and justice in the country. The authorities, with the support of the international community, urgently need to root out impunity and corruption, including within state institutions. It is also crucial to take meaningful steps to bring perpetrators to account for the grave human rights violations and abuses that have been committed. In addition, work needs to begin to address the country's pervasive inequalities and poverty. Madam Vice-President, the people of Haiti need the unwavering attention and support of the international community. All States need to implement the Security Council's arms embargo in full to prevent the illicit trafficking of firearms and ammunition into Haiti, and enforcement at borders is absolutely crucial. I urge States to support the Gang Suppression Force with sufficient funding and personnel. It is vital to ensure that robust human rights safeguards underpin its work. My office is ready to continue providing advice on the conduct of operations in line with international human rights law. We can and must turn this situation around for the people of Haiti. Thank you very much.
Thank you. I now give the floor to Mr. William O'Neil for his presentation by video.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for inviting me to this crucial meeting. I've been saying for quite some time now that Haiti faces the abyss. It is on the brink, that the situation is more than urgent. I sometimes feel like the boy who cried wolf, but this time I really believe it is a make or break moment for Haiti. I have worked in Haiti over many years, but I have never seen the situation as desperate as it is now. Most indicators are flashing red. Killings, kidnappings, sexual violence, and destruction of properties are crippling what is left of Haiti's delicate social fabric. This violence is no longer contained to the capital. It is now spreading across large swaths of the country. Gang violence is the primary cause, but I'm alarmed by an increasing number of reports of extrajudicial executions by the Haitian National Police and killings and other human rights abuses conducted by self-defense brigades and non-organized members of the population. Gang violence also means millions of Haitians face food insecurity and have limited access to health care, clean water, and education. They often must flee for their lives from their homes. Over 1.3 million are displaced, one of the countries with the highest percentage of its population internally displaced. The situation has an impact on areas far outside those controlled by gangs. The gangs impose hefty taxes on all goods moving through their territories. They also extort money from businesses and markets, which must pay or else. This raises the cost of everything for people who already are barely surviving. I interviewed educators and medical professionals in the north and south, and they had similar stories, overcrowded schools, impossibly high costs of all materials, medical supplies, and fuel. The main hospital in Geronimo depends on periodic donations of fuel from an NGO so that it could turn its generator on. They have not had electricity supplies for over three years. The recent incursion by gangs into northern Haiti is especially alarming, as it is very hard to see how the government, local and international organizations would be able to respond. And the North Coast is where most of the boats leave filled with Haitians seeking to reach other countries, including in the Caribbean or the United States. In addition to a potential surge of people fleeing violence by land, the crisis might propel many to attempt dangerous smuggling journeys in overcrowded vessels on the high seas. Religious leaders and civil society members have issued a heart rending call for help a few weeks ago following a gang attack on the town of Bassin Bleu. A young teacher, beloved by the community, was among those killed by the gang, who also burned his body. We need to listen to their appeal for help.

I continue to receive heart-rending testimonies from the population suffering from this violence, and I quote: We have nowhere left to go. Violence and misery generated by gangs is insidious. It seeps into every nook and cranny of our lives. Fear and hunger grip our stomachs. Gradually, gangs are extending their territory. After Port-au-Prince and the department of L'ouest, other departments and other towns are falling into the hands of armed gangs. That is in particular the case of Artibonite and the town of Mirabelais, and it will be the case of Bassin Bleu. How did we get here? What can we do to exit this situation?

These are the questions many Haitians are asking now. We need to try to answer them. It is our common responsibility. I hope during our debate here that we can rally the solidarity of the international community in support of Haiti. helping identify pathways out of this downward spiral so that Haitians may finally enjoy the peace and prosperity they deserve.

I therefore invite you all to strongly defend Haiti's cause in your respective capitals. You will have to deploy considerable efforts and secure the support of all stakeholders in all areas. But each and every one, we must be deeply committed to human rights and give Haiti a chance. Let us ensure that this is the last time Haiti needs such support. Thank you very much. I very much look forward to our discussion. The time to act is now.
Thank you. According to our practice, we shall start by hearing the delegation of the country concerned. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Haiti. You have five minutes.

Madame Vice-President, High Commissioner, six months ago I appeared before you to describe the situation in my country, Haiti. Today, I'd like to say that matters are better. Sadly, in many neighborhoods, the night of violence has still not given, or moved to give place to the dawn of right of law. Today, families live in fear. Today, the youth sees hope disappear. I thank the High Commissioner for his oral update and the independent expert for his work and the Council for its constant determination to monitor the situation. The reality is raw. About 6 million people, including a million children, millions of children, need immediate aid straight away. Over 5 million are in food insecurity, and 1.3 million are displaced, IDPs in fact, in their own country. Schools are closed and quiet. The plates are empty. Fear causes markets to close. The school textbooks are closed. The roads are not safe anymore. Behind every figure, there is a face behind every percentage, a dignity behind every statistic, a story we refuse to abandon. The state is acting sometimes behind, not in the limelight, but constantly, we have tried to stem violence, states of emergency that we targeted to prevent the people reorganizing our security situation to make our response more effective. The police has stemmed the flow of weapons. We've coordinated with the United Nations and our partners to reopen classes, reestablish his healthcare, secure access to water. Nothing is perfect, but nothing is standing still. Our government is doing what it can with the means it has, with the humble certainty that every. A day that we win over fear is a day we give back to life. We express our deep thanks to the UN for the recent allocation of $9 million by the Central Emergency Fund. 9 million gives us a breath of fresh air. That is water, shelters, classrooms. However, 90% of the humanitarian response plan is still not funded. We call upon donors to express solidarity towards the Haitian people and meet this call for funds. We also thank all states standing side by side with Haiti, and we'd like to mention in particular those delegations who have relayed Haiti's voice at the 80th session of the General Assembly at the podium. We also welcome the recent adoption of resolution 2793 of the Security Council. Solidarity is not just a word, it is an act which saves. Excellencies, The needs remain crying. Millions of children are deprived of the fundamental right to education. Millions of people are deprived of the right to health. Millions of families are deprived of their right to feed themselves. Millions of men and women are deprived of their right to live in dignity and in security. Because when you teach a child, violence wanes. When you heal a mother, the community breathes. When you feed a family, peace returns. We ask you to speed up your financial support to remedy the financial deficit to support humanitarian access. We live in paradoxical times. Humanity has never had as much knowledge, know-how and means, but yet the humanity deficit has never been so big. what cost we want to make progress, not at the price of millions of souls killed and dehumanization, but we do want to ensure that hunger ends up in museums, pollution in school books, and justice and discrimination in the archives of libraries. Today still, children die of malnutrition. Today still, children can't go to school. Today still, minorities are assaulted. Today still, women are oppressed. How long will we keep on saying, "Today still," quote, unquote. In all four corners of the world, peoples who are suffering call for just action based on solidarity. We're not asking you to do the impossible. We're asking you to do what is indispensable. We need resources that meet our humanitarian needs. We need life corridors for humanitarian aid. We need sustainable support and stabilization for and recovery. Let us build bridges rather than walls. Let us extend hands rather than point fingers, let us light lamps rather than multiply shadows. Kofi Annan reminded us we will not enjoy development without security, we won't enjoy security without development, we won't enjoy either without human rights being respected. After all, where do human rights begin? Eleanor Roosevelt reminded us, and I quote, "Human rights begin in small communities, in our neighborhoods, so close and so small that you can't see them on the map of the world." End of quote. That is where the future of Haiti is taking place, in the classroom, in the mobile clinic, return to the child and the mother, in the street where life is returned. Let us Chaos into calm, urgency into hope, assistance into effective rights, survival into a future. We owe it to our children. We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to the very idea of the United Nations. I thank you.

Thank you. The list of speakers is now closed. I now invite interested delegations to ask questions to the presenters and to make comments on their statements. I would also like to remind you that the speaking time is one minute, 30 seconds. I give the floor to Norway on behalf of a group of countries.

Thank you, Madam Vice-President. I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of the Nordic-Baltic States. We thank the High Commissioner and Mr O'Neill for their updates, and we remain gravely concerned by reports of ongoing and escalating human rights violations and abuses in Haiti. We reiterate our support for efforts to restore stability, rebuild democratic institutions, and ensure accountability. Sexual and gender-based violence has reached unprecedented levels. Rape and sexual slavery are reportedly used as tools of intimidation and control by criminal gangs. Women and girls, of course, are disproportionately affected, while the collapse of judicial institutions and systemic weaknesses in the rule of law leave survivors with virtually no access to justice or protection. And like you just pointed out, High Commissioner, and also our colleague from Haiti, the situation of children is particularly alarming. An entire generation is being deprived of their rights to safety and education. So there is indeed an urgent need for stronger international assistance, and we note the recent developments to this end. not only to curb the violence, but also to uphold human rights, protect civilians, including children, ensure accountability, support to victims and survivors, and facilitate the reintegration of children recruited by criminal gangs. High Commissioner, how can the international community best contribute to achieving these objectives? I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to European Union.

Thank you, Madam Vice-President, Mr. Vice-President, thank you. Commissioner, independent expert, the international community must help Haiti to put an end to the mass human rights violations and to restore the rule of law and democratic governance. The situation is extremely serious. Women and girls live under the permanent threat of sexual and gender-based violence. Children are victims of forced recruitment and are used by gangs. The EU supports the transformation of the multinational mission to support the security into a force to suppress gangs, as well as to the drug trafficking. On 15 July, we adopted new sanctions against the gang leaders. We, in 2025, will spend 20 million euros for humanitarian aid in Haiti. The EU supports the creation of lasting structures based on human rights, especially in the education public basic services and food security. We call upon the Haitian politicians to meet their responsibilities and to adopt lasting solutions for the future of Haiti. Mr. Commissioner, high expert, your work is useful to document the violations and identify and support Haiti in implementing the reforms it needs to implement. What will be the role of OHCHR in the new force created to suppress gangs, which has just been adopted, approved by the Security Council. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to Bahamas on behalf of Caribbean community.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the CARICOM group in Geneva. We thank the High Commissioner for his oral update and Mr. O'Neill for his insights. CARICOM joins in expressing grave concern over the deepening human rights, security, and humanitarian crisis in Haiti. The UN Secretary-General previously underscored that urgent, coordinated action is required to protect civilians and restore stability. CARICOM fully supported this call with a view to ensuring that any mission remains accountable, respects due diligence, and is integrated with Haitian-led institutions and civil society. In this connection, CARICOM foreign ministers on September 23, 25, expressed support for the draft Security Council resolution that proposed the transition of the MSSM to a strengthened gang suppression force, complemented by a UN support office. We therefore echo the statement made yesterday by the CARICOM ambassadors in New York, wholeheartedly welcoming the adoption of the resolution by the Security Council and underscoring the need to ensure sustainable, predictable sourcing of the GSF by all international partners. We also call for the urgent capitalization of the 2025 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan for Haiti. Caricom will continue to stand with Haiti in support of all Haitian-led solutions and to work with the UN and other regional and international partners in supporting the country on a path to lasting peace, to dignity, and to justice for the Haitian people. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to Dominican Republic.

Gracias. Thank you, Madame Vice-President. The Dominican Republic is grateful for the report, and we fully share the concerns voiced therein. For my country, the Haitian disaster is a share that affects us deeply, because we share the same island, as you know, and we have a common history also. The Haitian people is trapped in a multidimensional crisis in which human rights protection is the first victim. Millions have lost their dignity and their right to live in peace. That's why we support also resolution 2793 of the UN Security Council, which establishes the creation of a force to get rid of gangs with a clear mandate and under the supervision of the UN. This opens up a window of hope, but it will only have a transformative impact if it goes hand in hand with international solidarity and the resources needed to strengthen Haitian institutions as they endeavour to combat corruption, violence, and impunity, and guaranteeing, thus, the absolute respect for human rights and a peaceful political transition. Without justice, there will be no democracy nor free elections in Haiti. Its stability also means the stability of all our region. We need to act firmly, but with humanity. The Haitian people deserve to live free of fear and recover its hope. Thank you very much, Madam Vice-President.
Thank you. I give the floor to Jamaica.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. The Jamaican delegation thanks the High Commissioner and the experts on human rights for their sobering updates on the grave human rights situation in Haiti. Jamaica remains deeply concerned by the deteriorating security situation in our sister nation, the continuous internal displacement of people, as well as the numerous outward migratory trends, despite the deployment of the MSSM over two resolution cycles. We commend the High Commissioner's continued engagement and echo the call for a coordinated response for the protection of civilians, especially women and children, unimpeded humanitarian access, restoration of the rule of law and democratic institutions for accountability and justice. Jamaica is deeply encouraged by the increased advocacy for Haiti that has prompted the adoption of UN Security Council Resolution 2793, authorizing a UN support office in Haiti and the establishment of the GSF as the successor to the MSSM. We align the statement-- align with the statement just delivered by the Bahamas on behalf of the CARICOM group in Geneva. As a member of CARICOM, Jamaica reiterates our commitment to supporting regional and international efforts aimed at restoring peace, stability, and democratic governance in Haiti, including our role in the standing group of partners for the GSF. These are critical prerequisites if Haiti is to embark on a process of economic growth and development, build its resilience, and achieve prosperity for its people. This is our desire for Haiti and all Haitians.

Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to Mexico.

Thank you, my Vice President. Mexico voices its concern about the violence stemming from the use of armed weapons in Haiti, frustrating the exercise of human rights. We urge people to scale up efforts to combat trafficking, the unlawful trafficking of weapons to slow down the violence of gangs. We underscore the need to combat the participation of boys and girls and adolescents in gangs. through effective prevention and integration, social integration programs. We absolutely must adopt judicial programs and strategies to stop the killings, general violence, as well as corruption and impunity, which perpetuates the crisis. We hope that a multinational force to combat the criminal gangs, approved by the Security Council, will produce results. Also, a priority is to prevent, attend to, and sanction violence and gender-based violence, including the sexual exploitation, and guarantee at all times the rights of victims. Finally, Mexico restates its commitment to find sustainable solutions that strengthen security cooperation, democracy, and respect of human rights in Haiti. Thank you very much indeed.
Thank you. I give the floor to Chile.

My name is President. Chile is grateful for the update by the High Commissioner and the contributions from the independent expert. We voice our deepest concern about the scaling up of the human rights crisis in Haiti. According to the last, uh, binu report, there have been 1,500 deaths, 609 injured, 185 abducted, and 628 victims of sexual violence. These data confirms that there's a systematic pattern of abuse by armed groups, which use terror, sexual coercion, and territorial control to subjugate communities. In addition, internal displacement has reached dramatic figures of 1.3 million people have been forced to move inside the country. These and facts hurt most the most vulnerable, deepening the crisis of access to basic services such as education and protection. We welcome the adoption of resolution 2793 of the Security Council, which authorizes the transition towards a force to get rid of gangs, as a force to establish order and to permit conditions to organize credible elections. However, we underscore the fact that the operations of the mission must be adhere strictly to international humanitarian law and international human rights law, focusing in particular on protecting women, children, and vulnerable groups with robust accountability mechanisms. Finally, we urge the international community to remain vigilant and to support the Haitian people with effective assistance and sustained assistance at these critical times. Thank you.

Thank you. This was the last speaker we could accommodate this morning. Excellencies, distinguished participants, This brings us to the end of this meeting. We will reconvene this afternoon at 3:00 p.m. to continue the interactive dialogue on High Commissioner's oral update on the situation of human rights in Haiti, to be followed by the interactive dialogue independent expert on Central African Republic. I hereby close the 37th meeting of the 60th session of the Human Rights Council.
